claims.claim: A business is an organization that strives for a profit by providing goods and services desired by its customers — the working definition used in this lesson, attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Business (Section 1.1).
A business provides goods and/or services to interested parties in exchange for financial payment; the exchange of value is what separates a business from a hobby or a favor.

Goods are tangible items manufactured by businesses (such as laptops), while services are intangible offerings that cannot be held, touched, or stored; physicians, lawyers, hairstylists, car washes, and airlines all provide services.

Businesses exist because they organize production and exchange efficiently: the purpose of a business is to facilitate the economic production of goods or services, and using resources (natural resources, labor, capital) in a coordinated way lets an organization produce more with the same inputs.
Businesses create the goods and services that are the basis of our standard of living and play a key role in quality of life by providing jobs and goods and services to society.

Customers are the people or organizations that buy: businesses meet the needs of consumers (medical care, autos, and countless other goods and services) and also serve other organizations such as hospitals, retailers, and governments.

Revenue is the money a company receives from selling goods or providing services; costs are expenses such as rent, salaries, supplies, and transport; when revenue exceeds costs the difference is profit, and when costs exceed revenue the business shows a loss.

A not-for-profit organization exists to achieve some goal other than the usual business goal of profit (feeding the hungry, preserving the environment, funding medical research, running a community theater); it can still earn revenue and pay costs, with any surplus reinvested in the mission. Examples include charities, most hospitals, zoos, arts organizations, and civic groups; government is the largest not-for-profit group.
The concept of a business begins with an idea and a name; a working business is that idea plus the organization that delivers it — people, resources, processes, and paying customers.

Production — the conversion of inputs (natural resources, raw materials, human resources, capital) into outputs (products and services) — links businesses into a chain: a single purchase sits at the end of a series of organizations that each convert inputs into outputs and exchange them for payment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame the profit motive differently. OpenStax's working definition builds profit into the definition of a business ('strives for a profit'), while Investopedia's broader definition covers both for-profit and nonprofit entities as businesses.
positions: OpenStax: a business is an organization that strives for a profit by providing goods and services desired by its customers.

Investopedia: a business is an entity that provides goods and/or services to interested parties in exchange for financial payment; businesses can be for-profit entities or nonprofit organizations fulfilling a charitable mission or furthering a social cause.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a substantive conflict: both sources agree a business provides goods or services in exchange for value. The lesson uses the OpenStax working definition as the attributed core, presents not-for-profit organizations as a distinct class with a mission motive (as both sources describe), and states the profit motive factually rather than as a value judgment.
